JUDGES' ACT AMENDMENT Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 65, to amend the Judges' Act.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Residence within county court district.

Will the Minister of
Justice explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the law at present, judges have to reside in the county for which they have been appointed. In 1919 the province of Ontario enacted legislation for the purpose of ultimately increasing the number of county court judges. It provided that the Lieutenant Governor in Council had authority to group two or three counties into one county court district, and when one of the judges retired or died, he would not

Judges' Act Amendment

be replaced, but the business would be done by the remaining judge or judges. This has been done in a number of cases and the number of county court judges in Ontario has actually been reduced.
The object of this legislation is to authorize a judge who has been appointed for a county to reside at another place in the new district formed by the grouping of several counties, and to live there legally and be entitled to his travelling expenses from that place when he goes into the district which is constituted by the amalgamation of those counties.
Mr. CHURCH; What is the minister doing to reduce the number of judges in Ontario? There are 66 county court judges in that province. According to the Ontario government returns, there were 60,533 civil suits, of which about 28 per cent were in the city of Toronto where there are only six county court judges. There is a congestion in the Toronto district and I should like to know what the minister is doing in regard to it. His predecessor said that during the recess of parliament he would take this matter up and relieve this congestion in the county of York, but nothing whatever has been done yet to put the matter on a proper basis. We have about eighteen high court judges, three or four of whom at times can spend about six months' holidays on political commissions. If we are to have economy, let us have it in counties where there are two judges where there is not enough civil and criminal work for one judge. In some parts there is scarcely enough division court work for the county court judge, whereas in Toronto the work is congested. In view of the Ontario legislation, the minister ought to tell the committee what he is going to do respecting a reduction of the county and high court judges, especially when some of these high court judges can take holidays, sometimes two or three times a year, and spend months on political commissions.
Mr. BO\S:	I should like to make an
observation or two regarding what my hon. friend (Mr. Church) has just said. His knowledge of the work is probably confined, to some extent, to what takes place in the city of Toronto. My life has been spent in the country, and I can assure him that he is entirely in error if he thinks that county court judges are not called upon to perform a good deal of work. Any return that may be referred to at the present time will not, in my ^ opinion, reflect the true condition of affairs. Since the amendment to the County Court Act, in my county, and I venture to say in many other counties throughout 
Ontario, cases are and may be sued in the county court no matter what amount of money is involved, and unless the jurisdiction of the court is disputed, those cases proceed to trial in the county court. My own firm and many other firms in Simcoe are continually bringing actions in the county court where, as a rule, the jurisdiction is not disputed and the cases go to trial there. On account of that the county court judge has a great deal more work to do and, perhaps, two years from now the returns, when they are secured, will reflect that feature which they do not reflect at present.
I agree with what my hon. friend says in connection with the work in Toronto. There is no question that the county court judges there work very hard, and it may be that something should be done. Possibly the scheme which the minister has will relieve that to some extent by bringing in outside judges from time to time for use in Toronto. That was done in the past and it can be done in the future. But I do not wish to allow to pass unnoticed the statement that judges in the county courts in Ontario or elsewhere in Canada are not having a good deal of work to do. They certainly are. Our county is a large one and we have two judges. I think I may say that outside of the judges, perhaps, in Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa and London, they have certainly as much or more to do than any of the other judges and they are kept fairly well occupied. The returns as to cases are not reliable data to go upon. A judge in the country may have to travel twenty or thirty miles to try one or two division court cases, and if you look only at the returns, it would appear that he was having very little to do. It means, however, that he leaves his home in the morning or, perhaps, the night before, and he has to spend the whole day there for the convenience- and properly so-of the litigants in that particular place. A judge in Toronto leaves his home at half past nine, ten or eleven o'clock and sits in court until four, half past four or sometimes five o'clock in the afternoon and he is never away from home. That is a consideration that must not be overlooked. I venture to say that most judges would prefer to be engaged continually from ten o'clock to four or half past four in the afternoon and have no travelling to do rather than spend many days in the year away from home. I trust if any consideration is to be given to what has been said, the minister will bear in mind that feature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the first
part of the remarks of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) as to the congestion of work in the county of York, I may observe that this matter does not come directly under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice inasmuch as the organization of tribunals lies within the sphere of the province. There is no doubt that the judges of the county of York who are administering justice in Toronto have a considerably larger amount of work to do than have the judges of the other districts of the province. Applications have already been made that special treatment be given those judges in the way of increased salaries. It has also been represented that in the districts of Hamilton, London and Ottawa there is legitimate ground for special consideration. The matter presents some difficulty; as my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) himself admits, it would be somewhat unwise to discriminate between judges of the same jurisdiction and standing. There is no doubt, however, that especially in the case of Toronto where the judges are overwhelmed with work a larger salary than is at present paid is deserved. But I would hesitate to open the question of increasing judges' salaries at this session.
It would not be popular.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Laprairie and Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) applauds that statement; but the demand is being made and certainly it will have to be considered seriously. The present discussion, however, is hardly relevant under this bill. There was an agreement, about which I think my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) knows, between the previous government and the government of Ontario, when the salaries of county court judges were increased, that the number of judges should be reduced; and the province has enacted legislation to that end. The Attorney General of Ontario has indicated the districts which have been formed by the grouping of two or three counties where a
Judges' Act Amendment

lesser number of judges can do the work, and this has been the policy pursued both by the previous and the present government. Only recently there was in the county of Huron a vacancy which has not been filled, that county having been added, I think, to Perth to form a new district. There is therefore no longer any necessity for a judge in Huron and no new appointment has been made. The purpose of this bill is merely to determine the most convenient place in the whole district for the residence of the judge.
Is it not reasonable that when the readjustment takes place there should be an improvement in the salaries of the judges in the county of York, in view of the greater amount of work they have to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to have a
general expression of opinion as to whether that is advisable and whether it would be good policy to discriminate in the matter of the salaries paid to judges administering justice in the respective districts.

I agree with the minister that there is a good deal of difficulty about the question of adjusting judicial salaries, and that difficulty arises largely from the fact that our counties or judicial districts, particularly in the province of Ontario, are by no means all alike. There is a great disparity between the judicial districts; there is a great difference in their respective areas; there is a great difference in the facility or the difficulty of travelling from place to place; and there is also a difference in the population of one as compared with another. There are some counties in Ontario where one judge can perform all the judicial duties and have time to spare; but I do not think that is the case in the great majority of our counties. The Ontario legislature passed an act to overcome that difficulty by grouping certain counties for the purpose of reducing the number of judges and thus saving the extra cost in salaries to the country. There are counties like York where there is always a great pressure of business and where a very large proportion of the litigation in the province takes place. My hon. friend (Mr. Church) stated a moment ago that about 28 per cent of a certain class of cases arising in the province were disposed of in Toronto. The county in which I live is fairly compact and has a population of some 55,000. Hitherto we have always enjoyed the distinction of having two county judges, but after the passage of recent legislation in Ontario the number was reduced to [Mr. Lapointe.l
one. Simcoe county, represented by my hon. friend who sits behind me (Mr. Boys), has I believe a population of about 90,000, and territorially it is a very much larger county than the county of Wellington. Simcoe still has two county judges, and I maintain that there is as much work for one county judge, if not more, in the county of Wellington as there is for two in the county of Simcoe. At the same time, let me add, the two county judges in Simcoe perform in a year as much judicial service as do the county judges of the county of York. It would be very difficult under these circumstances to discriminate in the matter of judicial salaries. If the minister thinks that the time has come when there should be an increase in those salaries,, all well and good but I think that increase should apply to all county judges alike, whether they be in Toronto or in the most remote districts of Ontario. I for one am inclined to think that judicial salaries might well be increased. I am aware that there is no unanimity of opinion upon the point, and I am expressing only my own view. I think that the county court judges in this province are still underpaid. the high court judges likewise, but whether this is the proper time to advocate an increase in their salaries I do not know. This bill, however, is certainly a move in the right direction. When the legislature of Ontario grouped the counties, a difficulty arose as to where the judge was to be located, where we could expect to find him; and particularly is this bill necessary because it will fix the point from which the judge will base his calculations for travelling expenses. I assume that that is one of the important objects of the proposed measure.
There are a large number of judicial functions arising in Ontario under the Municipal Act entirely unconnected with litigation, such as questions of assessment and appeals from mimicipal assessments. Judges in Ontario are also police commissioners, in which capacity they have to perform duties of various kinds not altogether judicial in character. When all these extra duties are taken into consideration, I submit, judicial salaries in Ontario, whether for high court judges or county court judges, cannot 'be termed exorbitant, and I think the minister might well consider the propriety of some increase.

Is it correct that certain
judges in Montreal are paid higher salaries than county judges in the province of Quebec by reason of the fact that their expenses are greater in Montreal than they would be in the rural districts?

Judges' Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, the judges of the
high court ia Montreal are paid exactly the same salaries as the judges in the rural districts. My friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was referring to the judges of the circuit court; they are in a class by themselves and are not like the county court judges in Ontario, who have the same standing and the same jurisdiction all over the province. The circuit court at Montreal is a special tribunal with a special standing, and apart from the jurisdiction which my friend has referred to these judges have jurisdiction in all municipal matters, and it is well known by litigants and the bar that those judges have a very considerable amount of work to do. Their salaries are not as high as those of the high court judges, but, it is true, they are higher than the salaries of the county court judges of Ontario.

Two thousand
dollars more, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is.

Since there has been
taxation of incomes, have judges' salaries been increased at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think they have.

It follows from
what the minister has said that the legislature of Ontario ought to create a special court for Toronto.

Mr. Chairman, I know it
will appear somewhat audacious for a farmer to discuss matters pertaining to judges and lawyers, but I understand that the hon. minister has intimated that the judges are making a demand for increased salaries. I also understand that the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) upholds that viewpoint and thinks that an increase would not do any harm. In view of this, I beg to siibmit some figures contained in an answer to a question which I put on the order paper on April 14', last. I was informed that we have 280 judges in the Dominion. I do not know how that figure compares with the judiciary in other countries, such as the United States or England, but I venture the guess that we are overmanned in this respect as well as in respect to other governmental machinery. I was also informed that the annual salaries paid our judges in 1919 were $1,452,554.57. In 1920, I think in conjunction with the increase of parliamentary indemnities, the salaries of the judges were increased, the aggregate amounting to $529,845.43. The total salaries paid our judges now are $1,982.-
440. In addition to these salaries we also have to meet a bill for travellling expenses, which last year amounted to $134,623.47. Not only have we 280 active judges, but we have 38 on the retired list, these being in the fortunate position of drawing very remunerative pensions, the total paid them on this account last year being $179,166.63, or an average of $4,714.90. In view of the condition of the country I think we are paying our judges too much. There is a demand for economy all along the line, and it seems to me that, although many of these judges are eminent men deserving of all we can give them, they are also rich and should not expect such high salaries. I have been met with the argument that a good lawyer can always command a high salary. We have evidence that this is the case, for we know that our government will pay lawyers from $200 to $250 a day to take a case-yes, I believe in the case of W. N. Tilley they paid $400 a day. So there is no doubt something in the argument that good lawyers can get m ore-money in private practice than they would receive on the bench. I am taking this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to protest against any increase in judges' salaries.

Mr. Chairman, I have
searched this bill in vain to find anything in it in connection with salaries of judges, and I think that the whole discussion is out of order. Let me therefore practise economy in time by getting back to the subject of the bill. I should like to ask the hon, Minister of Justice if he would accept an amendment so that the section would read, "the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia." The conditions existing in British Columbia are parallel with those existing in Ontario, and if it is just and proper-and I quite believe it is-that the federal government which appoints the judiciary, should also designate the place at which they should reside within their district, then it is equally applicable to British Columbia. I do not know whether he is perfectly acquainted with the facts, but his predecessor in office was advised of conditions in British Columbia which rendered an amendment such as I have indicated very desirable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The matter has not been called to my attention at all. This bill is intended to meet special conditions arising in Ontario on account of the act which was passed by the legislature of Ontario in 1919 grouping together many counties for the purpose of the administration of justice. I do
Judges' Act Amendment

not know that the same conditions exist in British Columbia. The law as it is to-day compels a judge to live in his county, but we have to change it on account of the new conditions in Ontario. Has there been special legislation enacted in British Columbia organizing a new system of grouping of counties?

No, there has not been any grouping of counties; but this condition arose: in a certain district there was one county court judge, who resided, as the law provides, anywhere within the riding. Owing to the sparsely settled character of the district and the long distances to be travelled it was desired to have another judge to reside in the northern or more scattered portion of the district. After a great deal of agitation extending over a number of years this was granted and the second judge, when he was appointed, elected to reside not in the scattered portion of the district, where he was required and for the sole purposes of which he was appointed, but in the southern portion, a location more convenient to him. He is now drawing the salary, without being of any advantage to the government or to the lawyers or the people of the district wherein he resides. He really helps the other judge do what that other judge was quite able to do himself. He is within his rights, because he is living within the county. While this is not a question of the grouping of districts, the condition arises precisely there as in Ontario. The government is passing legislation here taking power to direct any judge to reside in any portion of his new district, or group district, as it may be. The principle is the same: you are not saying here that a judge shall reside somewhere in this group district, but that he shall reside at that point in his group district which the government shall designate. I submit that that is a parallel case, and that there could be no harm in taking similar powers in that respect to those now being taken for Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that what my hon. friend mentions is a condition which prevails only in one particular place.

So far it has taken place only in one county, because there is no other country district where there are two judges, but it is apt to occur at any place. One error is quite sufficient to justify our making provision for it, now that we are passing an act dealing with the matter. As the government retain the power in their own hands, no harm can be done if the government afterwards find it inadvisable to exercise that power. It is identically the same principle in British Columbia as in Ontario; it is a question of

the taking of power to designate the residence of a judge within his jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend should let this legislation go without the addition of the amendment he suggests. This is to meet a special provincial condition arising out of legislation applying to Ontario alone. I shall be pleased to consider the question submitted by my hon. friend and I assure him that if any legislation is necessary owing to the circumstances existing in the case to which he refers, we shall be glad to deal with the matter with a view to remedying the difficulty.

I am obliged to the minister for his statement. But ministers of justice have a habit of passing away sometimes. We have the bill; we have the grievance; the remedy is right here, and I suggest that no great harm would result if this bill were allowed to stand over for another day, with a view to amending it as I suggest.

I doubt very much whether the bill now before the committee would meet the situation in British Columbia. The bill is drawn precisely to meet a situation in Ontario which has arisen as a result of action by the legislature of the province. If the legislature of British Columbia passed an act similar to the legislation passed by Ontario I have no doubt that the bill could be amended as my hon. friend suggests. But until we have evidence that British Columbia has passed an act to apply the grouping system, I think it would be entirely inappropriate to amend a bill drawn especially for Ontario. I rose particularly to say a word in reply to the hon. member (Mr. Leader). I admit that the question of judicial salaries does not arise directly in this bill, and I only mentioned the matter in response to the invitation of the minister that the opinion of hon. members be given on the subject. I did have reason to look into the matter with some care in 1920 when the salaries of judges generally were increased. I found then what I think you will find to-day, that judicial salaries in Canada are far less than they are in Great Britain or in any other British dominion. There is no comparison between judicial salaries in Canada and those in the United Kingdom.
How does the number of judges in Canada compare with that in Great Britain?

I could not answer that;
I am speaking only of the amount paid to individual judges for the performance of their duty as judges. In England the judges are paid on such a high scale that we could not

Exchequer Court Act Amendment
consider it in this country; I admit that. But comparing the salaries paid in Canada with those paid in Australia, South Africa, even New Zealand, we found in 1920, and I think you will find still to-day-though I cannot speak in regard to the figures to-day, because I have not examined them-that the salaries of judges in Canada are substantially less than those of judges in any of the other self-governing dominions.

The legislature of Ontario has placed on the county court judges of York a volume of work which county court judges in no other province are required to perform. They have the work in connection with the assessment rolls, voters' lists, election courts, and so on. The duties of division court judges and a very large proportion of the High Court work of Ontario has been laid upon the county court judges. A great many of these judges work very hard. The county of York has about one-third of the population of Ontario, and one-third of all the writs issued in the province are issued in the civil courts of York county. But they have only six county judges out of a total of sixty-six in the province, so that six judges do one-third of the county' court judicial work of the province, while the other sixty do the remainder of it. Let me give a few figures to show why the Ontario government passed this cluster county district legislation. The county court judges of the county of York have to call for assistance from the county court judges of the county of Simcoe, the junior judge for that county and the senior and junior judges of Ontario, Halton, Peel and many other counties. Last year 5,430 county court writs were issued in civil cases throughout the whole of Ontario, while in the county of York 2,230 were issued, or 42 per cent of the number for the whole province. In Ontario there were 163 jury trials in county courts, and in York county 54, or 33 per cent. In Ontario there, were 705 non-jury trials, and in York county 273, or 35 per cent. The figures for the criminal cases are about the same. There are only three other counties that can compare with York in this respect, namely, Middlesex, Wentworth and Carleton. In Middlesex county in 1922 there were 19 judgments entered, amounting to a total of $4,447; in Wentworth, 56 judgments, amounting to $14,555; in Carleton, 18 judgments, amounting to $3,680; in York county, 317 judgments, amounting to $110,061, or half the mount-$220,000-registered for all Ontario counties. The idea of the legislation passed in Ontario must be to
transfer judges from districts in which the work is light to districts where there is a greater volume of business. A meeting of the county court judges was held last September and it was felt then that the county of York judges ought to be dealt with as a special case. In view of the fact that the late Minister of Justice promised that something would be done for York county judges,
I hope that action will be taken this session by the minister with a view to giving recognition to the men who do the work.

In view of the fact that
this is the 18th of June, I would ask if this discussion is in order, Mr. Chairman.

It may be in order,
but I am somewhat in doubt.
Mr. CLARK; Much has been said from the point of view of the province of Ontario.
I merely wish to express the opinion that discrimination at any time is a bad thing, and that if salaries in the city of Toronto, for instance, are increased for the county court judges, they should be increased in Vancouver and every other city of Canada, and I am not so sure that they should not be increased also in the rural districts.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 116, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On Section 1-jurisdiction conferred by agreement.

Will my hon.
friend explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 20 of the Exchequer Court Act defines the matters in which the court has jurisdiction. That section was amended in 1916 by the addition of paragraph (g) which reads as follows:
Every matteT in which the Crown and any person interested therein have agreed that the Crown shall pay to such person an amount to be determined by the Exchequer Court.
The purpose of this amendment is to widen the effect of this clause so that the court will have jurisdiction when the Crown and any
3336	COMMONS
Exchequer Court Act Amendment
person have agreed in writing that either the Crown or that person shall pay
4 o'clock an amount to be determined by the Exchequer court, and also in cases where any question of law or fact have been agreed upon in writing to be determined by the Exchequer court. To illustrate: when a contract is entered into by the Crown and any person, it may be stipulated in the contract that any difficulties arising out of it shall be determined by the Exchequer court, and this amendment is to confer jurisdiction upon the court to try such cases, where both the Crown and the person have agreed in writing, upon it. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Nothing of the sort is
contemplated. I think two judges, when they both work, are sufficient to look after all the work of the Exchequer court. My hon. friend will agree that it is desirable that matters in which the Crown is concerned should go to the Exchequer court; that is the natural tribunal to deal with all claims against the Crown or by the Crown arising for instance, under the Expropriation Act, cases for damages caused to property by reason of public works, cases under the Patent Act, and cases where there is loss of life by neglect of 
a servant of the Crown. And of course my hon. friend will see that these questions which may be submitted in consequence of an agreement are always matters in which the Crown has an interest, but I do not think they are so numerous as to multiply the work of the court.

I just wanted to get an assurance on that point. Of course, it is perfectly clear that the Exchequer court is looked upon as a tribunal fitted to look after all these claims against the Crown that my hon. friend refers to, and they can be referred to the Exchequer court under the law as it now stands; but questions of agreements and the like were thought to be questions which could well be looked after by the ordinary courts, and so different principles are applied to them. I am not saying but that this legislation may be perfectly all right and serve a useful purpose, but it will not serve a useful purpose if we are taking work from courts that are not now busy and are giving it to a court that is fairly fully employed. I think my hon. friend will say that the Exchequer court is a fairly busy court. I am not saying that the judges are overworked, but they are busy, and sometimes there is a lot of work put upon them.
I do not suppose my hon. friend's view is that this in any way discharges the jurisdiction of the regular courts. I mean, does he think that the Crown ought to be put in bar of an action? In the case of a contract which to-day would not be sufficient in the opinion of the law to confer jurisdiction on the court itself, because the jurisdiction cannot be conferred by agreement-my hon. friend gets around that by his admendment- would he think it proper that this jurisdiction so conferred should be treated in bar of an action in one of the regular courts; in other words, as something which would oust the jurisdiction of the regular courts?

speechtext: What is really being done in connection with the production of platinum at the present time? No doubt the minister is familiar with this subject. speechtext:
Some years ago I asked in this House whether there had ever been disclosed to the people of Canada the information regarding the precious metal content of the nickel ore which was being exported from this country. That information has not yet been disclosed. We have absolute control of that nickel ore including the precious metals it contains. and yet we are unable to find out what the percentage
Gold and Silver Marking

of that precious metal content is. I believe that the Right Hon. Sir Arthur Mond, who has a considerable refining plant in Wales, takes a large amount of our nickel ore and refines it in the Old Country, and so far the Canadian people, who have absolute control of the nickel ore in this country, have been unable to ascertain the percentage of the precious metal content of the ore that is exported. The subsidy was granted to Mr. Fraser personally, and he thereupon organized a joint stock company and assigned the subsidy to the company, and then subsequently the subsidy was assigned to the trustee, under the trust deed, for the benefit of the bond holders and the prospectus of the underwriters says that this is going to pay the whole thing.
The prospectus also says, if my hon. friend had read a little further, that they hope the freight traffic will increase by 50 per cent, and the passenger traffic by 100 per cent.

But that is in addition
to getting full pay for the boat from the government. That is velvet on top of the other.

We have control over the rates, and I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me that these people who are shut off from the mainland for six months of the year are entitled to the very best service we can give them during the months when there is an opportunity to communicate with the mainland.

There is another feature,
and that is the service between Pictou and Souris. Does the minister think it is good policy that there should be any more competition with the car ferry or the Prince Edward Island railway than there is to-day, and that the government should subsidize a private concern to enter into competition with the Canadian National Railways? That is a matter of policy upon which I would like to hear the minister express an opinion.

The call at
Souris is a help to the Canadian National
Supply-Steamship Services

Railways. A great deal of through traffic from the mainland goes to Souris and is picked up there by this boat and taken to the Magdalen island, and freight is taken back. It is benefit to the Canadian National Railway's, rather than competition.

That is freight for the
Magdalen islands?

And freight
for the mainland as well.
I do not follow the argument.
How could it be for the mainland?

From the
Magdalen islands.

Is the minister serious in
that? The broad gauge has not been extended to Souris.
But there is a railway there.
With a narrow gauge, and the freight would have to be trans-shipped at Souris and handled again at Charlottetown.

It does not
make any difference whether the railway is broad gauge or narrow gauge; it has to be trans-shipped from the boat to the railway just the same.

But there would be no
carload lots trans-shipped in that way.

It makes no
difference.

It means all this extra
handling at Souris and again at Charlottetown. I would ask how much traffic goes that way from the Magdalen islands?

The extra
handling does not add to the freight. The shipper gets the same rate.

But it adds to the cost
for the National Railways. I do not see how it is of any benefit to them. The National Railways could get the freight at Pictou.
This is a condition that exists, and there is no way of changing it.

The minister will have
time between now and eight o'clock to bring

down copies of the letters which were written to these ship owners inviting them to tender, so that we can get the names, the dates and so forth.
If the item carries I will agree to bring that down.

It will not carry now,
until that is done, although I do not purpose myself delaying the passing of the item.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before the committee rose at six o'clock I promised the right hon. leader of the opposition that I would lay on the table a list of the parties to whom the forms calling for tenders were sent and a copy of the tender, and I now comply with that request.

I do not want the item to be passed till I have time to go through this list. What I have gone through is not very illuminating. The call for tenders was sent to the secretaries of the boards of trade of Quebec, Montreal, Halifax, Pictou and Charlottetown. I wonder whether they were sent to the hospitals in these places.
Surely my hon. friend would not object to having these forms sent to the secretaries of the boards of trade in these different, cities?
I do not know what good it would do.
I suppose my hon. friend never had any dealings with boards of trade.

Not very much. I do not quite understand what they are sent there for. These forms were also sent to the Deputy Postmaster General at Ottawa, to the vice president of the Canadian National Railways, and to Mr. Teakle, manager of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, in case he would want to build another boat probably. They were also sent to Major Bell. I do not know that very much information can be obtained from this list. However, I have not had time to go through it.
Twenty-five or thirty other names are mentioned.

I know that, but why they would be sent to these people I do not know.

Supply-Steamship Services
I cannot understand my hon. friend objecting to them being sent to the secretaries of the boards of trade. They are some of the persons to whom the forms certainly should be sent.

I suggest to the minister that unless some hon. member wishes to discuss this item, he should go on with another item till I get time to read these papers. I cannot read them in a second.
Item stands.
Quebec, Natashquan and Harrington and other ports on the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, steam service between, $85,000.
Better tell us something about this service?
This is a weekly service between Quebec and the north shore.

How long has it been in
existence?
I have the record here for about ten years, but I understand the service has been in existence for twenty-five or thirty years.
Who has this contract?
The Clarke Steamship Company.

How many trips do
they make during the season?
One trip a week.

How much of this
amount is being paid for the transportation of mails?

The boats are compelled to
carry the mails free. There is no special item for the mail service. We insist upon them carrying the mails.

How many boats are
there? The item is $85,000.
Two boats.
One trip a week?
Yes, it is a long trip.

How many trips is the
boat supposed to make, in order to qualify for the subsidy?
One trip a week during the season of navigation.

Is there a check made on
those trips?
Certainly.

My reason for bringing
this matter before the committee is that I realize quite well that the people on the north shore are entitled to a good service but we often read in the press statements that they are not getting the service desired. If they get a weekly service while navigation is open there is certainly no cause for complaint. It seems to me that when the large sum of $85,000 is paid as a subsidy for that service pains should be taken to see that a weekly trip is made while navigation is open.

The customs officers certify
to the number of trips.

I assume that the season
of navigation does not last much more than six months, say twenty-five weeks. If the total number of trips made is twenty-five $85,000 seems to be a rather enormous subsidy.

Each trip is approximately
809 miles.
When does this contract expire?
When was it made?

Is it customary for
the department to give ten-year contracts?

It is done occasionally, but it
is not customary.

In 1922 how many tenders
were put in?
Who holds the contract?
The Clarke Steamship Company. The contract was running and the company agreed to improve the service.

If the company make
the trip on time, do they always make a trip each week?
Yes.

Is the minister aware
that last August the North Shore left the north shore with the mails, took a cargo and went to St. Pierre Miquelon? By doing that they were eight days late in arriving at Quebec. According to my information this has been done twice.

We have had no complaint
about the service and if my hon. friend knew of any violation of the contract it was his duty to file a complaint.
Supply-Steamship Services

I learned of this just
a short time ago, and even though I had known of it and had interviewed my hon. friend before the opening of this session, I do not believe it would have done me any good. I remember full well the occasion when I went to him to try to get a subsidy for a company that is now operating between Matane and! the north shore. I am very sorry, but I must say that the way in which I was received could be compared' with the treatment of a dog in a bowling alley. My hon. friend was so busy that he could not take time to listen to me so that I might tell him what I wanted. He told me that it was absolutely unnecessary for me to go to that trouble. I had petitions from different companies on the north shore, and he did not even give me an opportunity to show them to him. There were some from the Ontario Pulp and Paper Company, the St. Regis Paper Company and the Hudson's Bay Company. One of these petitions was signed by 89 others, and another by 62 others, and they asked that the mail be taken to Matane by rail and then from there by water to the north shore. The minister is giving a subsidy of $85,000 to the Clarke Steamship Company for the number of trips that they make and he has given them a contract for ten years, thereby eliminating any competitors for that period. We are now improving the harbour at Matane and making an attempt to serve those people and serve them well. Now that the people on the north shore are asking to come to Matane, I fail to see why the subsidy that I asked for cannot be granted. It seems to me that if my hon. friend will think this matter over and endeavour to be fair, as I hope he will be, and give the people who are asking for accommodation, the facilities they require, he will put into the supplementary estimates a certain amount so that the people who are now going from Matane to the north shore will have an opportunity of continuing their work. Will my hon. friend even dream of putting an amount in the supplementary estimates for that purpose?

I am sorry to hear an hon.
member speak in that way because if there is one minister who tries to see everybody, it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sure, when I tell the committee that I had interviews on three different occasions with the hon. member, he cannot claim that he was shown any discourtesy. I did not turn him over to one of my officials, I spoke to him myself about the matter, as I always feel that members are anxious to interview the

minister himself. If he did not have time to present his case, as he says he had not, in three visits, that is not my responsibility. I have upon every occasion shown the hon. member the greatest courtesy in anything that he has laid before me, and I am prepared to do so in the future as I have done in the past. The hon. member has absolutely no grounds for making the statement that I did not appear to have time to discuss the matter with him.

Such is the case for
I remember full well what occurred. The reason I applied to the minister was that I wanted to come to the assistance of the people of my district and the people on the north shore as well. As the matter stands to-day the freight is being taken down by rail oh the Canadian National railway and on the Canada and Gulf Terminal railway to Matane, thence by water to the north shore. The mail is all being taken over to Matane. The other vessel is not taking it down from Quebec. These companies have boxes in the post office at Matane where they receive their mail and it is being taken across by our boats. The Clarke Steamship Company is receiving the subsidy and the others are doing the work. I do not believe that is altogether fair and just.

I drew to the attention of the hon. member at the time, as he will remember, the fact that there was a railway service to Matane; that a dock was being built by the government and that I thought in view of the expenditure that was being made in his riding, he should at least wait before pressing his request until the finances of the country were in a better condition than they are now.

At the same time if
what I asked had been granted to me, we would have come to the assistance of all those people and as well we would have aided in the development of that district.

I might also remind my hon.
friend that if we had responded to all the claims we had1 from members of this House we probably should not have had a surplus this year.

That is the best joke
yet.

Is it usual to let contracts of this kind for ten years? My impression is that steamship contracts are usually let for periods of from three to five yearn.

Supply-Steamship Services

I have already stated at least
six times to-day that it is not the usual thing to let these contracts for ten years, but the custom was established under my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen).

Oh no. The minister
cannot fetch one contract which was let for a period of ten years while we were in power.

As I pointed out to the
leader of the opposition this afternoon, the contract was always let for one year previous to the time he came into power. His government made it five years and we merely doubled that. In other words, he increased the usual period five times whereas we simply double the length of time he established. It is not the usual thing to let these contracts for ten years; it is only under exceptional circumstances that this has been done.

This contract I understand was made in 1922, the first year this government wias in power. What were the exceptional circumstances that made it necessary to increase the time to ten years? Will the minister at the same time say whether the Clarke Steamship Company is the same company which is operating in timber and pulp wood in Quebec?
I have no knowledge of that.

What is the name of the
ship?
There are two, the North Shore and the Labrador.

Can the minister answer
my question now as to how many tenders were received when the contract was let? And what was the next highest tender?

The negotiations were carried
on with the minister iand the contract was renewed without tender.

That means that this
contract was renewed for a longer period without tenders being called for?
It was negotiated by the former minister for ten years.
Without any tenders?

Yes. I might tell the hon.
gentleman that these contracts contain a provision that parliament may decline to vote the amount any year.
That is a wonderful advantage for parliament to have, and it is astonishing that the minister should protect parliament in that way.

It is a protection for the
people.

The minister is protectionist all right; he reserves to parliament the right to vote the money each year. The fact of the matter is that when a contract is made, especially in a case like this where bonds are sold on the strength of that contract, it is just as easy for the camel to pass through the eye of the needle as it is for parliament to get out of its undertaking. The predecessor of my hon. friend adopted the habit, and I presume that for similar reasons the rotating system is adopted of changing ministers before the next estimates come along so that the actual minister can plead that he is guiltless.

I am not pleading that at all;
I am willing to stand behind the former minister.

That is all very well,
but it is altogether different attacking a minister's successor from attacking the minister himself who did all these things. The government has entered into a contract for ten years, in all probability binding future governments, and in so doing it is launching upon a course which neither it nor anyone else can defend. A five year contract is wholly different; it can only extend a short time into the term of the ensuing government or parliament. But ten years is a comparatively indefinite period, and for the government to tie the hands of parliament for ten years is without any defence at all. I notice too that in calling for tenders the government does not say that the contract is for so many years; it is left open so that the government may take whichever contract it chooses and say it is the best. The whole thing is open for the government to put its hands upon its favourites here, there and everywhere. Here is a case in which the government renewed the contract for ten years.

Let me correct the hon. member before he goes further. During his regime there was used the same form of advertisement for tenders as is used to-day; the number of years was not stated in it but it was left to the contractor to say for how long he would undertake the service.

The minister knows that
previous to this government's coming into
335o
Supply-Steamship Services

power no contract was ever let for a period of ten years; he himself admits that five years was the longest term of any contract up to that time. Now he has let a contract for ten years and he puts the advertisement in such shape that the government can fix a period of five or ten years as it sees fit; it can say that the advantage in having a contract for five years is that it will overcome some difficulty or other, or on the other hand that the ten-year contract will be advantageous in some other respect. As a matter of fact it simply does away with competition.

I would ask my right hon.
friend whether it is better to have a wide open contract or one in which the number of years is stated.

Ordinarily the contract
was just for one year.

It appears to me, as I
think it should appear to the committee, that it must be very poor satisfaction to the people on that shore who could get a proper service from Matane to be told that, because the government which was in office prior to 1921 adopted a certain system, therefore it must now be followed. If the government previous to 1921 did not do what was exactly right in any respect there is no reason why this government should follow suit. If this contract had been let for five years only it would expire in 1927 and the department could then call for a new contract to give a satisfactory service to the people of Matane and Nat-ashquan. As it is they are subsidizing this other route whereas a better service could' be secured.

Is it the policy of the department now when these contracts expire to renew them for periods of ten years? If that is not the policy, what is the justification in the case of this vote for the Magdalen islands service, no tenders having been called for ? This is a matter of principle.

Let me correct the hon. gentleman; the contract was not let without a tender in the case of the Magdalen islands. It -S not the policy of the government to renew* lontracts for ten years, but there are exceptional cases where the circumstances render contracts of that period unavoidable. The ordinary man will not invest a large sum of money in a service for only one year; he will undertake it only if he can secure a contract for a number of years.

Ml*. HANSON: That is the statement with regard to the north shore service, which does require a good type of boat, and the North Shore is a splendid boat. But why a ten-year contract? Is it to suit the convenience- of the contractor-a matter of assistance to him; or is it now the settled policy of the government in such cases?

Does my hon. friend say that
the term was extended in order to assist some-individual or company?

Why it is all assistance.
All these subsidies are assistance. What else are they?
These are the same contractors who were awarded the earlier contracts for this service by the previous government.

In the case of the Magdalen islands boat the subsidy was not only to assist, it was to finance the whole undertaking. There is no doubt the bonds were sold on the strength of the subsidy and on nothing else; the underwriters would not have been able to sell the bonds otherwise, because the only guarantee that the bondholders would have that their interest would be paid regularly and the principal met at maturity w'as in the subsidy. And1 not only that, the subsidy itself is part of the security of the bondholders.

Surely my hon. friend will not charge the government with knowing anything about the bond issue at all. As a matter of fact I understand there has been a bond issue of 8500,000, if I heard my hon. friend correctly this afternoon. The proceeds of that issue will help the contractors to carry out their contract. A short time ago I received a tender from well recognized shipowners who have been in receipt of the subsidy for the service to the West Indian islands for a number of years. If I remember rightly they asked that they be given a contract for ten years. We have the matter under consideration now. But it is not an unusual thing where a large amount is invested in the boat for a contractor to decline to assume the responsibility of such an investment as the capital required for a large boat, unless some assurance is forthcoming of a contract for a period of years.

Apparently the minister is not very familiar with the details. If he confers with the officers of his department he will find that in the case of the Lovat Steamship Company the minister was consulted at every turn. As a matter of fact, he had given his consent to the assignment of the subsidy contract.

Supply-Steamship Services
That is correct.

The file shows that the
department was kept informed of every step that was being taken. It contains a record of correspondence between the department and the solicitors of the underwriters with respect to the assignment of the subsidy as security for the bonds, so that the government might be said to have been parties to the whole transaction.
I know only of the letter asking us to agree to the assigning of the contract to the Lovat Steamship Company, and a further letter asking us if the assignment had been completed.

Did not the minister have
to consent?
What contract is my hon. friend referring to.

The contract with the
Lovat Steamship Company.
Does my hon. friend not know that that item has been passed?
When was the item passed?

I was waiting for the
hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmoreney (Mr. Casgrain) to renew his protest.
Mr. CANNON. He has eaten since.

I have no objection to
the vote passing. I am satisfied that I shall get the Murray Bay-Tadoussac service next year.

I thought something had
happened.
Nothing has happened.
I have not had the pleasure of seeing my hon. friend since six o'clock.
It might be done otherwise; these transformations take place rapidly.

Not being familiar with politics,
I do not know how such transformations are effected.

I have learned from
observation. For how many years was the other tender of 850,000, and from whom?

Ten years; from Young and
Burchell of Sydney.

For how long was the
tender for 824,000?
One year. That was for the old boat.
Did the minister see what they would do it for if they got it for ten years with the chance to sell their bonds on the faith of the tender?
No purpose would have been served by such a course, the boat was not at all suitable for the service.
Did the boat comply with the stipulations which were sent out?
No.
In what respect did it not?
It was a very slow boat, seven or eight knots an hour.
What did the tender form specify?
The contract was for ten knots.
No; I am asking what did the request for tenders stipulate.
It did not so state, but the contract was specific.
Nothing was said in the request for tenders? They would not know what the contract was to be until after the tender had been accepted.

The department thought the boat offered by the former contractors was not suitable for the service and the terms of contract offered were not acceptable. It had the right to refuse the tender. The rejection of this boat for this service necessitated the original call for tenders. They undertook to operate at a speed of twelve knots per hour.
That is the tenderers?
No, the contractors under the contract.

Of course, doing business that way the minister can give the contract
Supply-Steamship Services

to whom he likes. He asks for tenders, but he does not stipulate the speed of the boat. Then when he gets a tender offering to operate a boat at a certain speed, he puts in the contract that the boat must have that speed, and he awards that tenderer a ten-year contract at more than twice the rate that has prevailed for years. What traffic was carried this year? We have had this new boat in operation for considerably over a year now.
It is not in operation yet.
Oh, it is still being built?
Yes; the subsidy is being paid on the 824,000 basis.
According to the contract the boat should have been in operation. Surely things are not frozen up there yet?
The contractors are operating the service with the old boat until the new one is ready, at the same rate as heretofore, $24,000.
Then they have not fulfilled the contract. Under the contract they were to start with the new boat at the opening of navigation.
I suppose my right hon. friend knows that there have been several dock and shipbuilding strikes in Scotland which naturally delayed the building of the boat?
Can the minister tell us what freight and passengers were carried this past year? I want to see how the new boat gets along.
I gave the latest return to my hon. friend this afternoon. I think he will find it in Hansard to-morrow.

I never heard any return as to the passengers and freight carried, except for the years previous. For that year the figures were these: Passengers, 1,313; freight, 6,380 tons; live stock, 8; bags of mail, 4,003. The number of trips made was 59 and the subsidy paid $24,000. Can the minister give the corresponding figures for the year past.
I shall give the same figures that I gave this afternoon: Number of passengers carried, 1,675; tons of freight, carried, 4,009; live stock, 70; mail bags: locked, 2,734; tied sacks, 1,902.
Doing less business than the year before.

That is accounted for by the poor service

the very boat we have been discussing all afternoon.

I cannot understand it, because the year before it carried 6,380 tons of freight, this year 4,000 odd. If it could carry 6,000 the year before it could carry 6,000 this year if the freight was offered.
Last year it went by schooner and gasoline boat.

Has the minister any
more of these contracts pending-$50,000 contracts to political favourites?
My hon. friend has a complete list of the subsidies that are proposed for this session. There may be a few in the supplementary estimates, but he has the main estimates before him.

Item agreed to.
Quebec or Montreal, and Gaspe and ports on the south shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, steam sendee between, $30,000.
Who has this contract?
The Clarke Steamship Company of Quebec.
How many trips do they make a season?
Every two weeks.

I learned on the 12th of May of this year that last summer they used this boat for service on the north shore to Cape Breton and left the people without accommodation in the district that they should have served. The Tremblay, plying between Quebec or Montreal and Gaspe, did the work. Is it fair that the Clarke Steamship Company should receive the subsidy while the other parties do the work?

The report received by the
department indicates that the Clarke Steamship Company are giving a good service. The Clarke Steamship Company's boat is much superior to the other boat.

Does my hon. friend
know that when the Tremblay was built I got a subsidy of $8,500 for that same boat, to go from Montreal to Gaspe? Afterwards the Clarke people leased the Tremblay and did the work, so the boat was good. WThy should it not be good now? A subsidy of $15,000 was asked for the Tremblay and was refused. Why pay $30,000 when the others are ready to do it for $15,000?

The passenger accommodation on the Tremblay is very poor. It is generally speaking an inferior boat to that operated by the Clarke Steamship Company, at least so our officers report.

Supply-Steamship Services
Seemingly the Tremblay was giving satisfaction when the Clarke people leased it.
The Tremblay was used simply because it was the best boat that could be obtained at that time.

Item agreed to.
Rimouski and Pointe aux Outardes, service between, $5,000.
Is this a new one?

The new contract commences
this year.

Who was the member
powerful enough to get a new service when my hon. friend (Mr. Gasgrain) failed?
The need of the country.

This service was established
last year.

It is a new contract,
though. If it were the member for Temis-couata I could understand it, but he is not the member for Rimouski. What was the need for this new contract when there was none needed for Tadoussac?
The country is being developed rapidly and lumbering

Is this the reward for
speeches in Rimouski?

Speeches by myself? I have
not made any down there.
It is to facilitate my right hon. friend's trip when he comes to meet the local member.

That is very kind indeed. I hope, however, to be in the district and to disclose the simplicity of my life and the innocence of my character. I did read the last deliverance of the hon. member, but gauging it very much, I know, as the member for Dorchester did himself, I did not think it was worth a reply.

This is a newly
organized company, is it not?

It is a new contractor-J. A.
Fafard.
When was the contract given?
It is dated May 9, 1923.

Is it not a fact that
this company was organized only last winter?

I have no knowledge of the
organization of any company.

These people came
here after the opening of the session, and I find it rather strange that my hon. friend would go sixty miles further to give a subsidy to a company while refusing me what I came here to ask of him three weeks before the opening of the session.
He refused me, too.

Cannot the minister
answer the question?
What is the question?

Why is the hon. member for Matane being turned down? He did not put it in just those words, but that was the substance of his question. He said that he was here three weeks before the House opened, and that he had a first rate case, but got no consideration, and that somebody sixty miles further away, with no case at all, got consideration, and he is appealing to the minister.
The only answer I can give is that there is no political patronage in the department.
It appears not to be a case of looking after the constituency, but of the ministers looking after themselves.
Will my right hon. friend point to one case, just one, where the Minister of Trade and Commerce has looked after himself?
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has not any water in his riding, but the right bower case from Pictou looks suspiciously like it to me.

Item agreed to.
St. John and St. Andrews, calling at intermediate points, steam service between, $3,000.

I notice a decrease of
$1,000 in this item. I was not aware that the route was so profitable that the contractor could afford to get along with a reduced amount, but I commend the minister for saving $1,000 of the people's money. Is this the same company or a reorganized company?
The same company.

I understand that it was current in the city of St. John and the county of Albert that the minister, or the department, had threatened to take away this subsidy altogether.
Supply-Steamship Services
I told them they could have the contract at a reduction of $1,000. They threatened to withdraw, and I simply stood #by my original decision.
What were the considerations that moved the minister to reduce it by $1,000? I would like to know how well run the department is.
It is very simple. This company is showing a large profit, and I decided to cut down the subsidy.
I think the minister is to be commended.

Item agreed to.
St. John and Bridgetown, steam service between,
{1,000.
What company has this service?
The Bridgetown Steamship Company, of Bridgetown, N.S.

Oh, that is in Lunenburg
county?
No, in Annapolis county. I suppose my hon. friend noticed a reduction there of $500.

Item agreed to.
St. John and Digby, steam service between, $15,000.

Is this the Canadian
Pacific line from St. John to Digby?
Yes.

I never could understand why it was necessary to subsidize that line. It is part of the through Canadian Pacific route from Montreal to Nova Scotia, and I had always supposed from the very liberal patronage that the boat received 9 p.m. that it was a paying proposition; but I may be wrong about that. I quite agree that it is necessary to have a steamship service across the bay, and a daily service such as they give, and it is a very, very good service, but I cannot understand on what principle the subsidy is granted for that line. Is this in consideration of carrying the mails?

That is one of the considerations. I might point out that the Canadian Pacific have had this contract for a number of years, and each year it has shown a large loss. They were paid $20,000 at one time.

St. John, Digby, Annapolis, and Granville along the west coast of Annapolis Basin, steam service between, $2,000.

We all realize that one of the most vital questions before us today is that of markets-the extension and the preservation of markets when we once get them. That applies not only to agriculture, but to all lines of industry. We are bending every effort to extend our markets in every direction where we can find them. In order to retain those markets there is one fundamental principle that we must not lose sight of. Once we have found markets, we must place on them a good product, uniform in quality and in such shape that those who are our customers will know that the article that they are getting is according to grade or as represented.
The marketing of grain is of vital importance to agriculturists, not only in eastern Canada, but in western Canada, to agriculturists in Canada as a whole, and in order to show the situation as it exists at the present time, I wish to make several quotations from this report which I received in the mail only last night. This is the report of the commissioners appointed last year to take up the question of complaints received respecting the condition of grain shipments from Canadian ports and from United States ports in bond to Great Britain. This report is made, by Mr. Leslie H. Boyd, chairman of the j Board of Grain Commissioners and George Serls, Chief Grain Inspector for Canada. Onj page 3 of the report -it is stated that the commission was appointed on the 16th May, 1623. The commissioners left Quebec on the 26th May, 1923, and arrived in Southampton on the 2nd of June, journeying down to London on the same day. On Thursday, June 7, a conference was held with the Canadian, Australasian and United States committee of the London Corn Exchange. The

report gives the names of those present but I need not read them. The report continues:
The chairman stated the objects of the conference and called upon Mr. Anderson, the President, to open the meeting.
Mr. Anderson stated that complaints of admixture had arisen in regard to Canadian grain shipped through United States ports and that some time before a i deputation from this association interviewed the
I United States Consul-General in London and placed before him evidence in respect to a number of specific cases of shipments, in regard to which complaints had been made and which had been officially investigated by his association. He further stated the result of [DOT] this interview -was that the consul-general obtained some very valuable reports from various ports in the United States and which, in his opinion, bore out the contention that there is slackness in preserving the identity of Canadian -wheat passing through the United States.
Again I quote from page 4:
It was stated in general discussion that most of the complaints during the last eighteen months had been in respect to shipments from Baltimore and Philadelphia. It was further stated that if the elevator companies are directly interested in wheat, the admixture in shipments is hardly surprising. The wheat was handled in the United Kingdom by docks who have no interest in it, and they could not have any incentive to tamper with it.
Mr. Serls and myself carefully outlined the process of inspection at Winnipeg and the head of the lakes, describing minutely the unloading of the grain into the elevators at the head of the lakes and the loading out into boats at these ports, and explained to the members present that when the certificate was issued for the cargo loaded and the boats left for American ports, the authority of the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada ceased. We also explained to the meeting that the large majority of elevators in the United States, which handled Canadian grain, were private, and that Canadian grain going through these elevators for export was supposed to be properly bonded, a great many of them being owned by the American railways, and, in reply to a suggestion of Mr. Robinson that the above government should take steps to protect Canadian grain passing through United States' elevators, I pointed out that as Canada only controls her own elevators, this was a practical impossibility.
Further:
It was very gratifying to note that there was no complaint in regard to Canadian grain shipped through Canadian ports, and Sir Herbert Robson stated that the only satisfactory remedy must come from closer co-operation between Canadian and United States governments, and that the bonding arrangements must be tightened. This goes to show the necessity for handling our grain through our own Canadian ports. Passing now to page 14 of the same report, I want to quote just a brief paragraph with reference to Holland:

The grading of wheat was considered generally satisfactory. Another paragraph appears regarding recommendations :
From your observations and investigations we are satisfied that, although the complaints of grain passing through the United States' ports were not numerous,

they are of sufficient importance to endanger the value of Canadian wheat sold on Canadian certificates passing through these ports. The buyer or receiver is bound to take delivery of the grain on Canadian certificates whether it be imported through United States' or Canadian ports, the certificates being final and there being no redress.
These are the quotations which I wish the committee to consider. From these quotations we find that under present conditions it is absolutely necessary for us to make some effort to have our grain handled through our own government elevators, through our own Canadian ports, transported via bay ports or other landing places over our own Canadian National Railways, thus giving employment to our own Canadian people. I think it is only fair to place the matter before the government and in these few remarks to-night 1 am trying to stress the importance of this feature of our government elevators; I think it is highly necessary that we should handle our own grain over our own railways through our own ports. This is important not only from the standpoint of securing markets but also of maintaining the confidence of our foreign customers.
I have one more suggestion to offer and I do not want hon. members to think that in this I am speaking altogether from the point of view of my own constituency. Let me refer to the situation in the harbour at Calling-wood, one of the Georgian bay ports. We have there one of the best harbours in Canada with first class accommodation for the larger boats; last winter there were about 22 tied up in the harbour, some of them 600 feet in length. There we have also the Colling-wood Shipbuilding Company, which I believe is classed among the first of such concerns in the country. We have, too, dry docks fully equipped for all classes of repair work. We have also an elevator owned by the federal government, but it is altogether inadequate and out of date to handle the large quantity of grain that comes to this port. We are also fortunate in having two branches of the Canadian National Railways running to Montreal, one going via Toronto and the other by way of Allandale, Orillia and Cobourg. My plea to the government to-night is that they do everything possible to facilitate the handling of the grain trade through our Canadian ports and over our Canadian National Railway lines, thus giving work to our people and at the same time helping to extend the markets which we need so badly to-day not only for agricultural products but for every-

thing else. I would ask the government to include in the supplementary estimates this year, or if not, in the main estimates next year, a vote for putting the government-owned elevator at Collingwood in a condition to take care not only of the export grain trade from that port, but also of the domestic grain trade, as the mills and farms throughout central Ontario are supplied from Collingwood, and, as I have already said, the present facilities are not at all what they should be.

Yes.

I think the minister could
do a great deal of good for the grain trade if he would distribute all the information given in 'the reports issued by the chief grain inspector and the chairman of the Board of Grain Commissioners. I am afraid one trouble is that those in the Old Country who are buying our grain do not know the facts as brought out in those reports. The statement was made that those importers were compelled to take the grain from whatever source it might come, whether from the American seaboard or not. I very much doubt that. From what I heard those men say themselves, I gathered that they had ceased taking grain from certain American seaports for the very reason which has been stated here to-night. If the minister would have those reports on hand at Wembley, for instance, I think they would do a great deal of good. The British grain importers are very eager for such information, and I think by this means a lot can be done to have our grain pass through Canadian channels.

I suppose during the year at
least 100 individual farmers in the western provinces have addressed complaints to me, and in every case I have written a personal letter to the chairman of the Grain Board asking him to make an investigation at once.
