I think the minister misunderstood me. I am referring to importers in the British Isles who are buying our grain. Largely in initiative rests with them to say where the grain shall come from.

Any complaints that come to
us are investigated, because we realize it is of the utmost importance that we keep faith with the people in England to whom the grain is sold.

I think if the minister
waits until complaints are received he will not be doing the service that is in his power. If this information was spread broadcast in Great. Britain I think the maximum good would be accomplished.

Does my hon. friend know
that at the present time one of the members of the Royal Grain Commission is in England investigating any complaints that may be made to him?

I am aware of that, but
I know he will not come in contact with one-quarter of the grain people there. I am sure that if those reports were circulated over there they would do a great deal of good and the results would be well worth the expenditure involved.

Mr. Chairman, in London to-day there is what is known as the Canadian Importers' Association. If the gentleman to whom my hon. friend (Mr. Low) referred meets the members of that association he will come in touch with all the angles of Canadian trade. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and myself had an opportunity of addressing the association while we were in London. We found that they are anxious to get all the information possible to help them to increase their business, which is the importation of Canadian products. My hon. friend across the way (Mr. Ross) spoke about the exportation of grain through Canadian ports. We are all anxious to have this done. I think this is an opportune time for me to say that the route over which Canadian products will go is, in a measure at least, in the hands of the producers themselves. My hon. friend shakes his head. Well, I will put it in a milder way: If the Canadian producer is anxious to have Canadian products go through Canadian ports, he can use his influence to this end. Western farmers or dealers can have their export products sent through Canadian ports if they so route them. The rates to Halifax and St. John are the same as the rates through American ports.

When the farmer dumps his
grain down the elevator he loses control of it.

I grasp that, but if the
farmers of the West would use their influence to have their products sent through Canadian. ports I have no doubt that they could impress upon the man who is routing it the desirability of doing that. We can only develop our Canadian ports by community effort. I merely wish to throw out the suggestion as to the advisability of helping out in this direction in every way we can. It may cost the railways a little more to haul the traffic to Halifax or St. John, but they are bound to carry it the way it is routed. Without the co-operation of all Canadian citizens we cannot develop our Canadian ports.

Is the rate on wheat
the same, say, from Winnipeg to St. John as it is from Winnipeg to Portland by rail?
Mr. GRAHAM. Yes, the rates are tne same. There was a differential against Halifax until a few months ago, but that has been removed, and although it would be cheaper for the Canadian railways to haul to Portland they have to give the same rate to Halifax or St. John that they give to Portland. Now, send your products by Halifax and St. John and help us to develop our Canadian ports.

Well, it costs more to ship
wheat from Fort William to Port Colborne than it does to ship it from Fort William to Buffalo. The remedy for that condition rests with the government; if they will abrogate the coastal shipping law, then wheat can go from Fort William to Canadian ports as it now goes from Fort William to American ports. The minister suggests that we are all anxious to have Canadian grain handled through Canadian ports, but we are raising and shipping down to Fort William more grain than our Canadian boats on the lakes can handle. So [DOT] long as the present coastal shipping law remains on the statute book, about 40 per cent of our grain must go through United States channels. United States boats are not allowed to take our grain from one Canadian port to another Canadian port, so when a United States vessel loads grain at a Canadian port she must discharge it at an American port. That grain is lost to Canada; yet the government seems to think it must maintain that coastal shipping law. In the fall of 1922 some of our shippers were being penalized to the extent of 2 or 3 cents a bushel because they tried to have their grain handled through Canadian ports. Prominent grain dealers in western Canada were wiring this government
Supply-Grain Elevators

asking them to suspend the coastal shipping law so that thpy could ship the grain to Port Colborne at the same rate that they were paying to Buffalo. But the government made no move in that direction, and a lot of our grain which might have gone through Canadian channels was forced into the United States. Until this coastal shipping law is repealed it will be impossible for our grain to get out through Canadian ports, and until the people of eastern Canada realize that, the grain will continue to go through American ports no matter how much we get up in this House and talk about the desirability of keeping Canadian grain in Canadian channels.

A large proportion of
Canadian grain does go down as far as Montreal and thence to Portland, but it is possible for the western shipper to see that that grain goes to a Canadian port instead of to Portland. Leaving out the Buffalo end of it altogether, that would be a good beginning. I have advised the Canadian shipping companies to have their representatives go to western Canada to discuss this whole situation with the western people and if possible come to some arrangement by which the Canadian ports will be given a preference. This suggested abrogation of the coastal laws is a very big question. Canadian ships are not allowed to do any coasting in the United States, and we have to take some steps to protect our own interests. But it must be remembered that Canadian ports carry a lot of United States grain simply because the shipper works in unison with the dealer in grain in the United States. My idea is to get the western people and the Ontario people in the frame of mind that they will do their best, everything being equal, to have their grain shipped through Canadian ports. If that is done, it strikes me that it will be a much easier task to regulate the freights than if we all stand aloof and take the attitude that we are going to send through the United States if that is better. We do get large shipments of grain from the United States through Montreal, because that is a better way of shipping it. I realize that there are difficulties but I want to sound the note of the desirability of eastern Canada and western Canada getting together in this matter with a view to seeing what can be done; that rather than stand aloof and say it cannot' be done we should be ready to meet with each other with a view to seeing that it is done. I am inclined to think that it is possible to get our rates regulated so that it will not

be more advantageous to ship to Buffalo. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government are working along that line, but there are many difficulties in the way. We are anxious that our carrying trade should not be handed over to the United States. But the question of abolition of coasting laws does not stop at a ship of grain on the Great Lakes; it is very far-reaching. It is not merely a Canadian question, ibut an international question; it is ocean-wide, because the question has been raised by Japan whether a ship starting from Liverpool and landing in Canada is not engaged in coastal trade, both countries being members of the British Empire. So we have to be very careful how we deal with the coasting laws, because our carrying trade and that of the British Empire might be interfered with on a very, very large scale. This is a time when consultation and conference and good-will, each to the other, will bring about results very far-reaching, and I have advised eastern men not to stand at long range, but to send their representatives to the West to consult with them as to the advisability of .them shipping their grain by Canadian ports. I believe that if we go to work earnestly we can bring about results by which without any detriment to the carrying trade of the Canadian merchant fleet or to the farmers of the West we can get a very much greater volume of traffic sent through our Canadian ports than we have at the present time.

way.

In that case, it is
routed. The clause I referred to applies to unrouted freight.

There is mighty little
traffic that is not routed. You can understand how easily at can be routed if the shipper does not care which way it goes.

I thoroughly agree with the minister's contention.

In answer to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) who asked why there was such a great difference between lake freights between Fort William and Port Col-bome and Fort William and Buffalo, the last complete figures I have are for the year 1922, and they show a difference of .62, or about three-fifths of one per cent per bushel in favour of the Canadian port. Mr. Chairman, I do not want to talk too long at this time of night. At the same time, I would not like to let the occasion pass without the comment I think it deserves. In the Maritime provinces particularly, the words just uttered by the Minister of Railways and Canals will, I think, be heard with a great deal of appreciation, and I do not propose that the line which politically separates us on the two sides of the House shall prevent me in any way from expressing appreciation of the policy which he has just enunciated. It is distinctly good and distinctly Canadian, and, if I may borrow a phrase from another quarter of the House, a step in the right direction. We will be glad to have a great many other such steps taken.
'Without in any way detracting from what the minister has said, I w'ant the House to realize that St. John as it is to-day, ready, willing, anxious to carry as much of the trade of Canada as it can secure, and not I think unduly jealous of the other great port in the Maritime provinces, Halifax, could not so far as the Canadian National Railway is concerned take full advantage of the trade of the West if it were being forwarded in the direction of St. John to-day. By means of the other national railway, the Canadian Pacific, we are getting a share of it, and we are willing and would be glad to have that share increased, but I want to emphasize at this moment that it is the business of this country not to make expenditures for terminals in Portland, Maine, but to make those expenditures within Canadian territory, at Halifax and at St. John. The Canadian National Railway to-day has a small grain elevator on the eastern side of the harbour
of St. John. That elevator is used only to some extent; I doubt if it is used at all to its capacity. There is about one berth available in connection with that railway. You cannot handle any reasonable proportion of the trade of the West through such facilities as those. There is opportunity in the vicinity of the new dry dock, and it is said there is a programme of development to go on there to make the National Railways capable of carrying its portion of Canadian trade through this Canadian port. I would like to see that programme implemented by some equal declaration on the part of the Minister of Public Works.
I would also like to see on the other side of the harbour, on the western side, the opportunity of the Canadian Pacific railway to handle the trade of the West made greater by the actual construction of the breakwater to Partridge island, and the completion of the programme to which the government of Canada is solemnly bound by what is known in St. John as the tri-partite agreement. That agreement provided for the building of wharves by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the government in conjunction. It has remained a dead letter almost from the day it was executed, and yet until these facilities are provided, the spout is not sufficient to handle the grain. That is no reason why we should not ask to get it in the East; but it is the reason why we should come to parliament and try as patiently as we can to convince, not the government alone, but to convince the whole of parliament, the group from the section from which I am speaking as well as the group supporting the government and the group situated to my left, that there are real opportunities in the Maritime provinces for handling this business, and that it is only fair, just and right that a reasonable portion of the resources of the Dominion of Canada should be expended in making those ports fit for the handling of this business. Add to that the encouraging sentiment put forward and so well expressed by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to-night, and I think we can take a very decided step towards making a more united Canada than in the past.

I mean in the East. I beg

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) who sits near me was about to demur to that statement, and I was about to correct my statement even before I was corrected by hon. members on the other side of the House. I was pleased to hear the remark of the Minister of Railways to-night that the removal of the differential of one cent as against Halifax put the port of Halifax as a port to-day on the same basis as St. John and Montreal and on the same basis as Portland, New York, Philadelphia, Boston and New London. If that is so, there is no reason why the hundred per cent Canadian in the West, whether he be a grower of grain or a broker who ships it out, or whether he be a purchaser, should not be a hundred per cent Canadian in the East, and when he can get the same rate through the ports of Halifax and St. John in winter, as against Portland, New York, Philadelphia or Boston, he should utilize these Canadian ports for the purpose of transporting that grain to the Mother Country and to any other parts of the world where it 
is required. I say, Mr. Chairman to-night, as I said before, that if our Canadian people are not a hundred per cent Canadian, if they are not going to look after the development of their own ports, but are going to sacrifice the interests of Canada and prevent Canada from becoming a great nation for their own self aggrandizement, it is the duty of this government or any other government that is in power, to see to it that grain and other products are shipped through Canadian ports; and if these products are not shipped through Canadian ports, then the government should consider whether or not an export duty should be placed on products shipped through foreign ports. Consider what the United States is doing to-day. What is it doing? It is giving a differential over its railways on all freight that is going to :be carried across the ocean in American bottoms. They are a country of 110,000,000 people, and we have scarcely 9,000,000 people.
Did they not propose that legislation and afterwards withdraw it?

No. If I am not mistaken they attempted to withdraw it, and I understood that under the law it was held in abeyance, but it is their intention to put that differential into effect, in order to obtain the traffic for American bottoms. My hon. friend shakes his head. I may say that I read the report of the Interstate Commerce Commission, and I read the application that was made for the staying of those proceedings, but it was only temporary; it has been held in abeyance and is to come into effect later. Even taking the statement of my hon. friend, it shows what public opinion in the United States is to-day. It shows the tendency of the public mind, not only the mind of the public man but of all the people of the United States; and if that is the tendency and if that is the mind of 110,000,000 of people in that country, surely it is up to us as a Canadian parliament and as a Canadian people to see to it that we protect our Canadian ports, and that we send through Canadian channels that which will help to make our country great and prosperous. If we fail to do that we are recreant in our duty. My hon. friend on the other side laughs. It is all very well for him to take that attitude. He is living in a country where he does not care very much about the Atlantic ports. There are hon. gentlemen in this House and in this country living in our middle West who do not care whether the grain goes to American ports or Canadian ports as long as Providence gives them the soil, the rain,

Supply-Grain Elevators
the sunshine, and the season, enabling them to grow the crops and sell them to the broker, the question as to how they are transported from this country means little or nothing to them. But there is a principle involved; and I desire to say to my hon. friends that when we in the Maritime provinces entered confederation in 1867 we gave to this great country a Maritime frontage that otherwise they would have been without. The moment the St. Lawrence closes Canada as a nation is without a national eastern seaport. If the American governments and the American people put an export duty on Canadian produce going through American ports, where would the Canadian people be for six months of the year? We gave that frontage to this great Dominion, we gave up our right to enter into fiscal relations with the 110,000,000 people to the south, and now we are told that when the St. Lawrence is closed by Providence it is only right that Canadian products should be transported to Portland, New London, New York or Boston. Are we, the Maritime people going to stand for that?

Would the hon. member permit me to say that the other night I advocated the shipment of grain through Canadian channels as far as possible. No hon. member on this side of the House has made any such insinuation as the hon. gentleman is making at the moment.

I beg the hon. gentleman's
pardon. I prefaced it with the word "if." I said: If it was the opinion of gentlemen- I did not say who sat in the House, but I said gentlemen who lived in the Canadian West, the men that were growing the wheat. I do not desire to detain the committee; but it is only fair and right that as a representative of the East, I, along with the hon. member for St.. John City (Mr. Baxter), should have made this statement here to-night to show that we are alive to the interests of the Maritime provinces, and we are not going to quit either in this House or in this country until we get our right which is due us. When we have that we shall be satisfied, and you will not find us complaining either here or in the country.

In spite of some remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Finn), I may say that I have a very sympathetic appreciation of the statements made by all three hon. gentlemen who have just addressed the House; that is, I am a sufficiently good Canadian to want to see all the traffic, commercially possible, carried through our own ports
and over our own railways. I think the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) was hardly correct in stating that the farmers of the prairies had very much influence in routing their grain after it got east of Fort William. The men who ship their own grain route it to Fort William, and they can naturally say how it will go, either Canadian National or Canadian Pacific. But when the grain gets to Fort William, that is their market; but beyond that, practically all our grain is handled by the men who purchase it from the farmers, and they are the men who must be approached in the matter. No matter what our sympathy, whether we ship by car or in any other way, we have no control over the routing after the grain arrives in Fort William and is unloaded in the elevators there, When I was at home, I wondered at times, and since I have had the pleasure of an opportunity of visiting the ports of Halifax and St. John which, I saw, were fine natural harbours, I wondered why our grain went through Portland and other American ports instead of through our ports in the Maritime provinces. I discussed the matter at some length, and I began to realize why it was; that with all the goodwill in the world it is hard to buck against natural facts or financial, not theories, but actualities. From Montreal to Portland over the Canadian National Railways-and I presume all the grain going to any of these ports must go through Montreal 

the distance is 297 miles. From Montreal to St. John over the Canadian National Railways it is 743 miles and from Montreal to Halifax over the Canadian National Railways it is 843 miles. There is the reason in a nutshell. By the Canadian Pacific-this does not apply to Halifax, but it does to St. John-the distance from Montrael to St. John is 481 miles. There is the reason. The cost, it is true, to the shipper is the same. That is, there is exactly the same rate from Montreal to any of those ports; but you can quite understand why the railway itself, which is supposed to show an operating profit, chooses the shorter route. There is the physical fact that we are up against. That is the disability under which those Canadian ports are labouring. I wondered over this many times, as I discussed the matter with gentlemen I met in those eastern ports and as we discussed it on our way home. Sympathetic and anxious as we were to see those ports prosper, we discussed many times how, through our co-operation or in any other manner, that disability could be overcome.

The distance is greater than
from Montreal to Portland, but the rate is
Supply-Grain Elevators

the same as to St. John and Halifax. If the railways were prepared to haul and time was mot a great factor, what is the argument in favour of Portland as against St. John and Halifax in the winter?

I said that from the
point of view of the shipper, unless time was an element, it made no difference which way the grain was routed. From the point of view of the railway which receives the same money for hauling a much greater distance, you can readily see why they, bound, if possible, to show an operating profit, would, as a business concern, prefer the shorter route. That is my point.

The distance from Montreal
to St. John over the Canadian Pacific is 184 miles further than the distance from Montreal to Portland. Why would the Canadian Pacific haul 184 miles further to St. John? Why would they not go to Portland?

I am not quite certain
whether the Canadian Pacific has a definite connection to Portland.

And the Canadian National
should not have either. If we have, we should not use it in order to ship Canadian products.

I have no intention
at this time of night of entering into an argument with the hon. member for Halifax as to the advisability of owning the American portion of the National Railways. That is a rather large subject. As to the righteousness of utilizing it if we do own it, that is a rather large subject again. I was simply pointing out, as best I could, where the difficulty existed. I am not pointing this out through any lack of sympathy, because if you are going to meet a problem, you must understand the problem. My sympathy is with Nova Scotia. I like Nova Scotia things. I went and got a wife from Nova Scotia, and I could not have paid that province a greater compliment. There is the problem, and there is no use in closing our eyes to the fact that a difficult problem exists and that the president of a railway, whose connection with the railway is a purely business concern, who is bound, if possible, to make this railway pay so as to reduce deficits to the vanishing point, to produce a revenue and to pay interest charges, is justified from his standpoint of view in using the shortest, most economical route and the route that will bring him the most money.

Has the hon. member considered also the factor that has not been mentioned yet, namely; that the ocean rate from New York and Boston-I am not sure about Portland-to Liverpool is about two cents better than the rate from Canadian ports?

I am aware of that fae,., but I had not quite come to that point because I was still on dry land. I was discussing the problem of the railway in moving the grain to the port. A number of us, anxious, although we live in the Middle West, to see the best done for the whole of Canada, were discussing and considering how that difficulty could be met. To my mind it is an unfair thing to say to a railway that is struggling to overcome a deficit: You must, at the same price received, haul grain a much greatei distance at a much greater cost. There is also the additional factor that, on the whole, the grade is better to Portland, and again that there is more return freight from Portland. Those are factors which you cannot overlook, and from a railway point of view the argument in favour of Portland is incontrovertible. Then comes the other point -in what way can you meet that difficulty? I am not advocating this; it must be a matter of government and not of railway policy. But to my mind there is only one thing that could be done; the government might say, "It is in the national interest that we should ship through these ports and that they should be developed." But are we prepared to subsidize the railways to pay the difference? I am not advocating that. I am simply saying that this is the only sound business way of approaching the matter, and it is useless to try to camouflage things and to blind ourselves to the situation. Are we prepared as a country to subsidize the railways to pay the difference in the cost in order that the grain may go through these ports? At the present time I have not made up my mind that this is wise and I am not going to offer the government any advice; I can only say that I am thankful that the responsibility is not mine. That, however, is my point of view. Eventually grain and merchandise must go by the way it can be carried cheapest, from the business point of view; and if the business point of view and the national point of view conflict, as they may do in this case-and I am not saying that they do-then the matter is one not

of railway policy but of government policy.
It is not a policy for the business men and the railways to initiate; the government must meet the situation.

I am able now to add a few
figures to those I have already given the hon. member (Mr: Coote). I stated that the Fort William to Port Colborne rate was less by three-fifths of a cent than the rate from Fort William to Buffalo. I should correct that; it is lower; it is two-fifths of a cent. The rate for the year 1923 for seven months, amounted to 3.63 to Goderich and 4.36 to Buffalo, a difference of three-quarters of a cent less to Goderich or bay ports than to Buffalo; and from Fort William bo Port Colborne it was a quarter of a cent less in 1923 than to Buffalo. These to the Canadian ports are lees than to American ports.

I must admit that the minister has the advantage of me in quoting figures in regard to lake freights because I have no figures before me to answer him. But I would suggest to the committee that if we could find as much discrepancy in these figures as occurred in those the minister quoted before we might discover that a wrong impression, if I might put it as strongly as that, had been created in the committee. I regret I have not here the report of the royal commission which examined into the matter of freight rates on the Great Lakes in the year 1922. I am sure I could show to the minister that the rates to Buffalo early in that season were one and a quarter cent less than to Port Colborne and that specific complaint in regard to that was made by Mr. James Stewart. He asked the government to suspend the coastal shipping law so that he might not be penalized by paying this high rate which made it difficult for him to compete with American millers. This government absolutely refused or neglected to suspend that law in 1922. If I had the correspondence which was brought down that year between the government and the different parties in regard to this suspension I am sure I could show the minister that the rates to Goderich and bay ports were much higher than they were to Buffalo, although the distance to Buffalo is several hundred miles greater.
There has been a good deal of talk here to-night regarding the question of the shipment of grain from Montreal to Atlantic ports, but that is only a very small percentage of the grain which is going out of Canada through Buffalo, and through Buffalo to the
different American ports on the Atlantic coast. The one great fact which must not be overlooked in connection with this shipment of grain through Canadian channels is that so long as this shipping law remains on the statute books 40 per cent of our grain-and I think I am placing the estimate very low- is forced to go through American channels. It cannot go to Montreal to have even the chance then of going through Halifax or St. John. I think that possibly we have dwelt on this question long enough; I presume that most of the members of the committee at this hour of the morning do not care to pursue the subject much further. But the question of the mixing of Canadian grain is one which must de dealt with and placed in a more satisfactory position than it occupies at the present time. Last year, in the month of July, Canadian wheat was 10 cents a bushel lower on the Liverpool market than Australian wheat, although we are always told in this House that we have the best wheat in the woTld. In conversation with a representative of one of the largest milling firms in Great Britain I was informed that in his opinion one of the reasons was that the Canadian grain which they bought could not be depended upon to be up to standard. He said that if our farmers could form a strong enough pool they could place their own inspectors at the elevator from which the grain left Canada, place their own inspection certificate on that grain, and1 place an agent in the Old Country who would examine the grain when it went there, and if any claim were made that it was not up to standard, the grading and sample could be made good to the English buyer. If we did that, he added, we could raise the price of our wheat, because, as he said, there was no question in the world that a lot of the grain they bought in England had been lowered in grade or sample.
This is one of the most important questions in connection with the grain trade, and so long as the bulk of the wheat which is going through Montreal is American wheat there is danger of the cargoes which go from Montreal being tampered with as well as the cargoes which are going from the United States. I want to impress upon the minister that I have been assured that the grain which has gone from Vancouver has so far been on an average of a better sample for the same grade than the grain going through Montreal. This goes to show that it is possible that the grades which are going out of the elevator at Montreal are not in all cases what they should be.

It is not my intention, to discuss the matter at any length at this hour, but there is one point that has not been discussed this evening. We all agree that the routing of Canadian grain through Canadian ports is a matter of great importance. I would like to point out to the Minister of Railways, who dealt with this question a few minutes ago, a remedy which would in a great measure prevent our grain going through American ports; that is, the routing of a great deal of it through the port of Vancouver. He could lend a great deal of assistance to this end by using his influence to have the mountain scale of freight rates reduced in proportion to the rates prevailing in other parts of the country. The minister told us this evening, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), that while the distance from Montreal to Portland is only 297 miles, as against 743 miles from Montreal to St. John, that the railways give exactly the same rate in both cases. And while the distance from Calgary to Fort William is 1,280 miles, as against only 640 miles from Calgary to Vancouver, yet we have to pay practically the same rate for the shorter ha,d; This in my opinion is a gross discrimination, especially against the people of Alberta because of the fact that Vancouver is their natural outlet. Although about two years ago only half a million bushels of wheat went through the port of Vancouver, this year already over fifty million bushels have been exported from that port, amply demonstrating that it is a feasible route. Last year Alberta produced 167,000,000 bushels of wheat, and every bushel of it for export would find its natural outlet through Vancouver, as would also a great portion of the Saskatchewan crop. The diversion of this wheat to the western route would relieve the eastern route to such an extent that it would be able to practically take care of all the grain that would naturally go through our eastern ports, and thereby render unnecessary the use of the American Atlantic ports for this purpose. I think the Minister of Railways will agree with me that through the Yellowhead pass the Canadian National Railways have as easy a grade as will be found on any other part of the road in Canada. Therefore in my opinion there is no reason why we in the West should be discriminated against by the mountain scale.
I trust this matter will be given careful consideration with a view to our getting the same treatment in regard to freight rates as is enjoyed by our friends in the East. I am entirely sympathetic with the aspirations of

our Maritime ports, and I should like to see every bushel of grain that is going out from the Atlantic seaboard handled through those ports to the fullest possible extent; but I believe the natural outlet for a great portion of our western grain is through the port of Vancouver, and I think this route should be given every encouragement.

I agree very largely with the remarks made by the hon. member for Red : Deer that the individual farmer loses coni of his wheat once it reaches Fort William, when the buyer determines the i route which it shall follow. I know from per-j sonal experience that the seller of 400,000 or ; 500,000 bushels of wheat immediately asks i how the buyer wants it routed. So the in-j dividual farmer, if he is shipping a car load through to Montreal or to Halifax or even across the ocean, is given this opportunity of saying how he wishes it routed; but the individual farmer undoubtedly loses control of his grain once it reaches Fort William.
